The stack hands the settings to the driver. `createExecutionStack` calls `RuntimeDriverDescriptor.create(options, sessionSettings)`, and `createControlStack` passes them in the control driver's connect options. The driver ensures every connection it hands to the runtime has them, whatever its binding. How it does so is the driver's choice. The PostgreSQL driver sends them as startup options on connections it opens. On a pool or client the user supplies, it applies them with a statement before first use, and again after an exclusively held connection is released, because the holder may have reset the session.
A codec never sets a session setting. If a connection does not have the setting, for example because a pooler dropped it, the codec refuses the value it cannot read and names the setting.

+A target declares a setting here only when a driver can set it at connection start on every server, including through a connection pooler. A setting a codec needs that cannot be set that way is a requirement on the database: the target does not declare it, nothing sets it, and the codec refuses a value printed under another value of it. PostgreSQL's `lc_monetary` is one. The `money` codec reads the text PostgreSQL prints under the `C` locale, but a per-transaction pooler refuses a connection whose startup options name `lc_monetary`, and a statement that sets it there changes a server connection other clients share. `DateStyle` differs on both counts: PgBouncer and the Prisma Postgres pooler accept it at connection start and keep it per client, so the statement the driver runs on a pool the user supplies stays with that client. Other poolers are untested. The target declared `lc_monetary` until 2026-11-20 (amended then; see "Money" in [ADR 254](ADR%20254%20-%20Data%20types%20and%20casts.md)).

## Money

-`money` is printed in the session's `lc_monetary` locale, whose currency symbol, separators and sign vary. The target declares `lc_monetary=C` beside `DateStyle=ISO`, and the driver ensures both the same way, so PostgreSQL prints `$1,234.56` and `-$1,234.56`. `pg/money` stores digit text with two fraction digits, `"-1234.56"`, and `pg/money@1` reads the `C` form into it exactly. It also reads a plain numeral such as `12.50`, which is how PostgreSQL reports a default written as a number, and refuses any other form with `RUNTIME.LC_MONETARY_NOT_C`. PostgreSQL also reads `money` input by `lc_monetary`, so under a German locale `12.50` would be stored as 1250.00. The PostgreSQL adapter therefore sends a `money` parameter as `numeric` and casts it, `$1::numeric::money`, which reads no separators; the cast is adapter policy, like every parameter cast. The conversion still scales the value by the number of fraction digits `lc_monetary` gives, so a write is exact under `C` and under every locale with two fraction digits, but not under one such as `ja_JP`, which has none. PostgreSQL has no conversion to `money` that ignores the setting, so `lc_monetary=C` stays a requirement for writes too. The setting also changes how `money` prints in an application's own raw SQL.

It also reads a plain numeral such as `12.50`, which is how PostgreSQL reports a default written as a number, and refuses any other form with `RUNTIME.LC_MONETARY_NOT_C`.

+The target does not declare `lc_monetary` as a session setting, and Prisma does not set it on a connection the runtime uses. It did until 2026-11-20, as a startup option beside `DateStyle=ISO`. A per-transaction connection pooler, such as the pooled address of Prisma Postgres, refuses a connection whose startup options name `lc_monetary`, so no client could connect through one, whether or not it used `money`. A statement cannot set it there either: it lands on a server connection the pooler shares, and other clients then read under it. So the setting is a requirement on the database: its `lc_monetary`, from the server's configuration, the database or the role, must print the `C` form. `C`, `POSIX` and `en_US` do; `en_GB` prints `£1,234.56` and `de_DE` prints `1.234,56 €`, and a read of either fails with the error above. The fix is `ALTER ROLE ... SET lc_monetary = 'C'` or the same on the database.

+PostgreSQL also reads `money` input by `lc_monetary`, so under a German locale `12.50` would be stored as 1250.00. The PostgreSQL adapter therefore sends a `money` parameter as `numeric` and casts it, `$1::numeric::money`, which reads no separators; the cast is adapter policy, like every parameter cast. The conversion still scales the value by the number of fraction digits `lc_monetary` gives, so a write is exact under `C` and under every locale with two fraction digits, but not under one such as `ja_JP`, which has none: there `1234.56` is stored as 1235 units. Nothing forces the setting any more, so on such a database a write is stored in the locale's units until the first read fails, and if `lc_monetary` is then changed to `C`, the rows written in between read back as wrong amounts with no error. The error and the upgrade instructions say so. Sending the parameter in PostgreSQL's binary format would close this, because `money`'s binary input reads the stored count of cents and ignores the setting. It is not done: no codec sends a binary parameter today, and a codec's one wire value also serves each element of a list parameter and a default written into DDL, which need text.

+The control plane owns every statement it runs, so it sets `lc_monetary=C` itself and needs nothing of the database. Introspection pins it with its other output settings, and the migration runner sets it locally in its transaction, so a `money` default is read and stored the same on every server. An application's own raw SQL prints `money` in the database's own form.
## Assembly
- **Enum member names in a default as string values.** A member name is a reference to a declaration, resolved in scope like a field name.
- **A vector type casting from the JSON type.** It matches on storage shape; a vector is several numbers.

- **A role name for the argument of a constructor every SQL target contributes**, such as `sql.Varchar`'s length declared `dataType: 'wholeNumber'` and resolved by each target at assembly. It is a small vocabulary of family types, which this ADR rejects above. The family builds the constructor with the target's size type instead (`sqlTargetTypeConstructors({ sizeType })`).

-- **Reading `money` through a `::numeric` cast in every query instead of setting `lc_monetary`.** A numeric cast prints the same text in every locale, but each read of a `money` column would need it: in a plain select, in a returned row and in a nested relation's JSON. No codec can add SQL to a read today, so every codec descriptor would gain a hook for one type.

+- **Reading `money` through a `::numeric` cast in every query instead of requiring the database to print the `C` form.** A numeric cast prints the same text in every locale, but each read of a `money` column would need it: in a plain select, in a returned row and in a nested relation's JSON. No codec can add SQL to a read today, so every codec descriptor would gain a hook for one type.

+- **Setting `lc_monetary=C` as a startup option on every connection.** This was the decision until 2026-11-20. A per-transaction connection pooler, measured on the pooled address of Prisma Postgres, accepts `DateStyle` as a startup option and refuses `lc_monetary`, so every connection through it failed.

+- **Setting `lc_monetary` with a statement on every connection.** Every direct connection would pay a statement for the pooled case, and through a per-transaction pooler the statement sets a server connection that other clients share.
+- **Connecting again without the startup options when the server refuses them.** The driver would have to guess why a connection failed, and a guess that is wrong hides the real failure.

+- **A client option that says the URL reaches a pooler.** The user would have to know which of their environments need it, and `money` behind the pooler would still need the role or database setting.

- **A SQLite data type that holds a whole number as a JavaScript number, for type-constructor sizes.** No SQLite column has such a type. `sqlite/real` already holds every size exactly, and a written whole number casts to it.

- **A framework number classifier that knows Decimal128.** The framework cannot depend on `bson`. The MongoDB target wraps the shared classifier with its own round-trip check; a number entry's `classify` is a plain function.

- **A MongoDB number with a fraction is a `mongo/double`, as the MongoDB shell reads it.** A double loses digits before the receiving type sees them. A fraction is a `mongo/decimal128` when a Decimal128 holds it exactly, as Postgres reads it as `pg/numeric`, and `mongo/double` casts from it. A number no Decimal128 holds exactly is a `mongo/double`, so every Double member accepted before stays valid.

## Introspection session settings

-Postgres prints a `timestamptz` value in the session's time zone, and dates, intervals and `bytea` values in the session's styles, so the same stored default can read back as different text on two servers. The adapter therefore runs the whole introspection read with `TimeZone = UTC`, `DateStyle = ISO, MDY`, `IntervalStyle = postgres`, and `bytea_output = hex`, and restores the caller's settings when it finishes, including when the read fails. Inside a caller's transaction the settings are set and restored locally; outside one they are set and restored for the session. Column defaults, check constraint text, index predicates, and policy expressions are all read under those settings, so their text does not depend on the server, the role, or what the caller had set.

+Postgres prints a `timestamptz` value in the session's time zone, dates, intervals and `bytea` values in the session's styles, and `money` in the session's monetary locale, so the same stored default can read back as different text on two servers. The adapter therefore runs the whole introspection read with `TimeZone = UTC`, `DateStyle = ISO, MDY`, `IntervalStyle = postgres`, `bytea_output = hex` and `lc_monetary = C`. The settings are always local to a transaction, so they never reach a server connection that a connection pooler shares with other clients. Inside a caller's transaction they are set locally and the caller's values are restored locally afterwards; outside one, the read runs in a transaction of its own, which is rolled back. Column defaults, check constraint text, index predicates, and policy expressions are all read under those settings, so their text does not depend on the server, the role, or what the caller had set.

+The migration runner sets `lc_monetary = C` locally in its transaction for the same reason: PostgreSQL reads a `money` literal in DDL, such as `DEFAULT '12.34'::money`, by the monetary locale, and `C` stores it exactly.
